articles.title: Understanding Voice AI Audio Formats and Quality Settings
articles.excerpt: Why Audio Formats Matter in Voice AI When you generate speech with a text‑to‑speech (TTS) engine or a voice‑cloning model, the raw audio data is just a sequence of numbers. To ship that data over the…
articles.body: Why Audio Formats Matter in Voice AI When you generate speech with a text‑to‑speech (TTS) engine or a voice‑cloning model, the raw audio data is just a sequence of numbers. To ship that data over the web, store it in a database, or embed it in an app, you need to wrap those numbers in a container format (MP3, WAV, OGG, etc.) and decide on quality settings (bitrate, sample rate, channels). Choosing the wrong combination can lead to: Clipping or distortion if the sample rate is too low for the model’s output. Bloated files that waste bandwidth, especially on mobile. Incompatible playback on browsers or devices that don’t support the chosen codec. Understanding the trade‑offs lets you deliver crisp, natural‑sounding voice AI without blowing up your storage bill.

articles.title: I Stopped Running Headless Chrome in CI and Just Use an API Now
articles.excerpt: tags: webdev, testing, cicd, screenshots Had a pretty standard setup: Puppeteer in a Docker container, running inside GitHub Actions, taking screenshots for visual regression tests. It worked. Mostly.…
articles.body: tags: webdev, testing, cicd, screenshots Had a pretty standard setup: Puppeteer in a Docker container, running inside GitHub Actions, taking screenshots for visual regression tests. It worked. Mostly. The problems were always the same: Chrome would randomly crash on larger pages, especially SPAs with heavy JS Memory usage was unpredictable. Some runs needed 2GB, others 512MB Font rendering differed between local and CI because of missing system fonts The Docker image was 1.2GB and took 45 seconds just to pull I spent way too long tweaking launch flags. `--disable-dev-shm-usage`, `--no-sandbox`, custom viewport hacks. Every few weeks something else would break. What I switched to Moved the screenshot step to an API call. One HTTP request, get back a PNG or WebP.

articles.excerpt: This morning a submission on the front page said that a widely used runtime had disappeared from GitHub. I have not verified that, and I am not going to build an argument on whether it is true. What m…
articles.body: This morning a submission on the front page said that a widely used runtime had disappeared from GitHub. I have not verified that, and I am not going to build an argument on whether it is true. What makes it worth writing about is that the sentence describes a failure every team has already pinned somewhere, and almost none of them can tell you which of their pins would break if it happened to them tomorrow. A build does not break because the upstream code changed. It breaks because something you wrote three years ago hardcoded an address that a stranger stopped serving — and you found out from a red CI run at the worst possible hour, months after the address moved.

articles.title: Overlap-Proof Cron: File Locks with O_EXCL and Stale-Lock Self-Healing
articles.excerpt: Windows Task Scheduler has no concept of mutual exclusion between runs. If you tell it to fire a job every 15 minutes, it will do exactly that, whether or not the previous instance is still alive. For…
articles.body: Windows Task Scheduler has no concept of mutual exclusion between runs. If you tell it to fire a job every 15 minutes, it will do exactly that, whether or not the previous instance is still alive. For a job that normally finishes in 10-30 seconds, this rarely matters. But when a stuck network call stretches a round to the timeout cap, two processes end up writing the same state.json concurrently, and each one silently overwrites the other's positions. The result is a corrupted state file and positions that vanish or double. The fix is a lock file created with O_EXCL , plus a staleness rule so that a killed process can't wedge the scheduler forever. This post walks through the implementation, the failure modes, and a small test suite.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.title: No more asteroid landing: Engine trouble forces Japan's Hayabusa2 probe to change plans
articles.excerpt: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 asteroid mission, due to problems with the spacecraft's ion thrusters.
articles.body: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters. The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu . Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.

This challenge asks for conceptual ideas about life in 2075 across four challenge topics. articles.title: China rolls out rocket for launch of 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station (video)
articles.excerpt: China has rolled to the launch pad the rocket and spacecraft for its Shenzhou-24 mission, which will fly the first international astronaut to the nation's Tiangong space station.
articles.body: China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut. A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week. The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026.
